x.ASV: A Song of Ascents. I will lift up mine eyes unto the mountains: From whence shall my help come?
x.Darby: A Song of degrees. I lift up mine eyes unto the mountains: whence shall my help come?
x.KJV: A Song of degrees. I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help.
x.YLT: A Song of the Ascents. I lift up mine eyes unto the hills, Whence doth my help come?

nt: The psalmist is using **lift up my eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to look up at” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I look up]

The psalmist is using the question form to set up a confident answer that he provides in verse 2. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I know where my help comes from!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [someone to help me]

x.ASV: My help cometh from Jehovah, Who made heaven and earth.
x.Darby: My help [cometh] from Jehovah, who made the heavens and the earth.
x.KJV: My help cometh from the Lord, which made heaven and earth.
x.YLT: My help is from Jehovah, maker of heaven and earth,

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The one who helps me is Yahweh]

The psalmist is referring to all of creation by naming two extremes, **heaven** and **earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all creation]

x.ASV: He will not suffer thy foot to be moved: He that keepeth thee will not slumber.
x.Darby: He will not suffer thy foot to be moved; he that keepeth thee will not slumber.
x.KJV: He will not suffer thy foot to be moved: he that keepeth thee will not slumber.
x.YLT: He suffereth not thy foot to be moved, Thy preserver slumbereth not.

nt: By using **May**, the psalmist is expressing what he desires or prays will happen. See the discussion in the introduction to Psalms about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that he will not give your foot to the slipping; that your keeper will not slumber]
The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, who was named in verse 2. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers as is modeled in the UST.

The psalmist is speaking of experiencing danger or hardship as if it were a person’s **foot** **slipping** and causing him to fall. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you over to danger]
The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the one who keeps you safe. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the one who keeps you safe]

x.ASV: Behold, he that keepeth Israel Will neither slumber nor sleep.
x.Darby: Behold, he that keepeth Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.
x.KJV: Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.
x.YLT: Lo, He slumbereth not, nor sleepeth, He who is preserving Israel.

nt: The psalmist is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Pay attention]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [he will not slumber, indeed, he will not sleep]
The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the one who keeps Israel safe. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the one who keeps Israel]

x.ASV: Jehovah is thy keeper: Jehovah is thy shade upon thy right hand.
x.Darby: Jehovah is thy keeper, Jehovah is thy shade upon thy right hand;
x.KJV: The Lord is thy keeper: the Lord is thy shade upon thy right hand.
x.YLT: Jehovah is thy preserver, Jehovah is thy shade on thy right hand,

nt: The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were **shade** that protects a person from the heat of the sun. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is your protection]

The psalmist is using **upon your right hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean “at your side” or “close beside you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at your side]

x.ASV: The sun shall not smite thee by day, Nor the moon by night.
x.Darby: The sun shall not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night.
x.KJV: The sun shall not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night.
x.YLT: By day the sun doth not smite thee, Nor the moon by night.

nt: The psalmist is speaking of **the sun** and **the moon** as if they were living things that could **strike** a person and cause harm. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the heat of the sun will not harm you, and the moon will not harm you by night]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the moon will not strike you by night]

x.ASV: Jehovah will keep thee from all evil; He will keep thy soul.
x.Darby: Jehovah will keep thee from all evil; he will keep thy soul.
x.KJV: The Lord shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul.
x.YLT: Jehovah preserveth thee from all evil, He doth preserve thy soul.

nt: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will protect you from all evil, yes, he will keep your soul]

The psalmist is using the adjective **evil** as a noun to mean evil things in general. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [from all evil things]
The psalmist is using one part of a person, his **soul**, to mean all of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your very life]

x.ASV: Jehovah will keep thy going out and thy coming in From this time forth and for evermore.
x.Darby: Jehovah will keep thy going out and thy coming in, from henceforth and for evermore.
x.KJV: The Lord shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore.
x.YLT: Jehovah preserveth thy going out and thy coming in, From henceforth even unto the age!

nt: The psalmist is referring to all of a person’s activities by naming two extremes, **your going out** and **your coming in**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you safe everywhere you go]

The psalmist is referring to all of time by naming two extremes, **now** and **forever**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for all time]
